history.heading: Three islands
paragraphs: The Caribbean Netherlands consists of three islands: Bonaire, off the coast of Venezuela, and Sint Eustatius and Saba in the northeastern Caribbean. Bonaire was inhabited by the Caquetío people before Spanish and then Dutch colonisation in 1636; the Dutch used it for salt production with enslaved labour.

Sint Eustatius, nicknamed "the Golden Rock", was one of the busiest trading ports in the Caribbean in the 18th century. In 1776 it became the first foreign place to salute the flag of the newly independent United States. Saba, a small volcanic island, was settled by Dutch, English and Scottish colonists.

history.heading: Becoming part of the Netherlands
paragraphs: The three islands were part of the Netherlands Antilles from 1954. When that country was dissolved on 10 October 2010, they became special municipalities of the Netherlands itself.

culture.heading: Distinct island cultures
paragraphs: Bonaire's residents mainly speak Papiamento, while English is the main language on Sint Eustatius and Saba; Dutch is official on all three. Bonaire is famous for diving, with its entire coastline protected as a marine park, and for flamingos. Saba is known for its steep mountain, Mount Scenery, and lace-making tradition.

politics.heading: Special municipalities
paragraphs: The islands are "public bodies", special municipalities of the Netherlands, each with an island council and a governor. Dutch law applies with some adaptations, and residents vote in Dutch national and European elections. They are not part of the EU but are overseas countries and territories associated with it.

economy.heading: Tourism and services
paragraphs: Tourism is the main source of income, especially diving on Bonaire and Saba. Bonaire also has salt production and an oil terminal, and Sint Eustatius has an oil storage terminal. The currency is the US dollar. Living costs are high, and poverty is a concern for some residents.
